title: The two scientists: hammers and nails
text:
I’ve recently come across an interesting proposition: scientists can be broadly classed hammers or nails. What I mean by this is that hammers are defined primarily by their tools, or the approaches they use to tackle a problem or question. The nails have a very specific problem (or set of problems) and try to bring a broad range approaches to solve them. A good example of someone who optimized the hammer approach is John Von Neumann, the mathematician who played a role in many of the most influential scientific projects of mid-century physics. He was a mathematician and brought is unique talent to bear in a range of problems, from the Manhattan project to the foundations of computer science. The prototypical nail is perhaps Charles Darwin, who spent much of his life investigating the diversity of life, developing the theory of evolution through decades spent breeding and cataloguing the plethora of life he encountered.
Of course this is not so clear cut and one can be a mixture of the two, rather this is a way of thinking about the way you approach scientific problems (or indeed any research project). Consider how you yourself start new projects. It is a valuable exercise to see how your own habits shape your research, because there are pitfalls to be aware of in both paradigms. The concern primarily is about not being bogged down; one can spend too long learning new things for the sake of it, thinking one is making progress because learning a new tool. Concurrently, one could also flit from one problem to another frequently, never settling on one long enough to actually make a dent in it. This is the value of thinking about research in this way, to be cognizant of the errors in process that just lead to a waste of time. There is a comparison we can make with Aristotle’s law of the golden mean - excess in either direction can be detrimental. Too much hammer and one is holding a solution and constantly looking for a problem. Too much nail and one never solves anything, because one is so wedded to a particular problem you can’t move on, even if it is the right thing to do. Just leave aside and move on to greener pastures.
A question might be when to apply each paradigm? Is it reasonable to to stick to one throughout your career? I would hazard to say that early in your career it might be worth learning a range of different methods, and this would imply the ‘nail’ approach, particularly as you are finding your niche, the subfield in which you build your reputation and scientific ‘portfolio’. Most researchers begin their career in a PhD program where we are provided with a problem, or at least sat within a larger group in which we have limited freedom to choose our problems. In this sense it is advantageous to begin in the ‘nail’ paradigm at the start. Once we leave our PhD and start as a post-doc we are generally then expected to be capable at certain key skills within a larger scientific program, but now we are experts in a particular technique. Often this is why we were hired to that new group as a post-doc in the first place. This is where the hammer-style of research comes in. Later on, when one has obtained a grant or more independence the freedom that comes from this enables you to pursue your own approach.
The question now however is the relative merits of both approaches. The severe expectations of a modern scientific career require a considerable output of grants, papers and talks to build a reputation and find a permanent position. There is a very real emphasis on quantity in modern science. Being a hammer or nail is thus refracted through the need for productivity to the detriment of originality or creativity. Perhaps I am pessimistic; experiences vary considerably across fields and countries. In this position the ‘hammer’ paradigm might be advantageous. You can apply yourself to many different projects, potentially building a large and impressive portfolio of results. On the other hand, the complexity of modern science and the interdiciplinary nature of advanced research projects favours those that can build a novel approach to hard problems. Here the ‘nail’ approach is at an advantage, because one can pull several techniques towards a well defined goal. A underemphasised virtue of a well defined problem is how it plays in grant writing. If you can clearly define your project goals then funders may be more ameanable to opening the purse strings.
A final question then. What do you think you are? Is your current approach to research questions suited to your skills and experience? Would aligning youself to one or other of these paradigms help you?

title: A Scientific Project Template
text:
I have found it helpful to have a standard template with which to start my projects; knowing where to start is the hardest part of any research project. I have created a simple science project template that I hope others might find useful. The scientific project template provides a structured starting point for organizing your project. It emphasizes keeping all files in one place and using version control with Git and GitHub for backup management. Embarking on a programming-based science project, or indeed any modern research project, requires good management of sources. The key to success lies in proper organization. Feel free to fork or clone the repository, changing it for your own needs. This template is for a python project, but the structure can be easily adapted to other popular scientific programming languages like MATLAB. Below I will go through the structure and workflow, including how I use git and Github to backup my work.
I have worked on different kinds of programming and research projects in the past; I have found the conventional project structure used in programming projects is ill-suited to scientific projects. Even if the project is heavily programming-based, science projects still need a way of tracking data, literature, plots, a labbook, and the eventual writeup.


Let’s start with a look at the folder organization. The key is to keep everything you need in one repository, with all code, plots, lab-books, notes and Jupyter notebooks together for easy reference. Keep all related files—data, scripts, documentation, and results—in a single folder or repository. This ensures everything is easily accessible and reduces the risk of losing important components.

Use clear naming conventions for files and folders to make navigation intuitive.
Maintain a clear directory structure that separates raw data, processed data, scripts, and outputs.

The template had the structure listed below. I will go through each part and explain the workflow, but feel free to delete or add whatever you need.
.
├── README.md
├── env.yaml
├── labbook_template.md
├── lit_rev.md
├── paper_skeleton.md
├── plots
├── run_project.sh
└── src
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── lib.py
    ├── notebook.py
    └── script.py
Firstly, all code projects should have a basic README file. This is a simple file describing the repository - what it’s for, who wrote it and the most important information for starting to use the repository. This is the information you see when looking at repositories on GitHub, and are standard practice for all programming projects.
The env.yml file is an anaconda environment file which describes the dependences and anaconda environment setup for the project. Programming-based science projects often involve numerous dependencies. Using environments can help you manage these effectively. For Python projects, Anaconda environments are highly recommended as they allow you to isolate dependencies for each project. While Python is the standard in scientific programming, tools like MATLAB or Julia may also be used depending on your field. Anaconda environments are the standard in scientific fields, particularly for those working in python. Python has certainly become the standard for all scientific programming and analysis tasks in recent years. Although MATLAB is still very popular and Julia has a lot of fans. Environments are your friend, and although one does not expect most scientist to be experienced software engineers, they can be a lifesaver when dealing with a plethora of competing dependencies.
The labbook_template.md is a simple markdown - formatted labbook to record your research as you go. There are a range of electronic labbooks available that you can use instead, but I still prefer a simple text-based file. The key is as always to keep a record of your work for yourself more than anything. The lit-rev.md is a template I use for reviewing preliminary literature. The paper_skeleton.md is a template for outlining the project and eventually helping to draft the resulting paper. The plots directory is self-explanatory, a place to keep all the important plots for your paper.
The src folder contains all the python code you write for your project. This includes Jupyter notebooks, python scripts and python library modules. These can be structured however you need, but in general I have found it is unnecessary to hew too close to proper programming practices when doing scientific projects. A final useful addition is a data folder in which you can keep raw data, processed data and results.



Start with the literature; as you go through the relevant literature, fill in a short entry for each article.
REFERENCE

objective
methods
key results
conclusions

Finally write a short summary of the literature you have reviewed to give yourself an overview of the most important references.
Once you have a plan and have a good view of the literature you can start with a few simple questions, I have included these in the paper_skeleton.md file.

What are you doing?
What is the context for this work?
Why is it interesting?
Where does this work follow from?
What are the key references of this work? (e.g. Smith et al. 2017)
What does the field need?
How does this improve on previous work?
What methods are being used?
Describe the data you are using
What are your results?
What do your results mean in context?
What are your conclusions?
How has your work fulfilled what the field needs?
How would you describe the narrative of this work?
What is a possible title of this work?
Write an abstract for your work
What possible journals are there for this work?

As the project proceeds fill each of these questions. Eventually you should be able to quickly write up a draft of you results. On the programming front, keep all your scripts and jupyter notebooks together, keeping track of all your plots and keeping everything in a simple logbook to track the progress of your project.
Any project will involve running and rerunning scripts, analyses and plotting functions as you go on. For this purpose I use a simple bash file. This bash file of terminal commands is helpful for multi-step processing and analyses. This is particularly important with regard to reproducibility; the ability to quickly repeat the whole analysis pipeline from the raw data is valuable for anyone trying to recreate your work. For example:
mkdir data
cp -r old_data data
python script1.py
python analyse_data.py
python plot_output.py



Git is a tool for managing changes in your project, while GitHub provides an online platform for hosting repositories. It might be a little unnecessary for scientific projects, but the ability to backup you work and version control long projects is incredibility valuable. The key value however is in collaborative projects; if you are in a team working on a large project, the branching and cloud backup ability of git and Github is no less useful for scientists than it is for programmers. You can take a look at the Github website or any of the online resources if you want to find out how it works. Version control systems like Git can be essential for scientific projects because they:

Track every change made to your files, ensuring transparency and reproducibility.
Facilitate collaboration by allowing multiple contributors to work on the same project simultaneously.
Provide a safety net by enabling you to revert to previous versions if errors occur.




Starting a programming-based science project requires careful planning, organization, and the right tools. By following these steps—organizing files, utilizing version control, documenting thoroughly, managing dependencies with environments, automating tasks, backing up regularly, and fostering collaboration—you can streamline your workflow and ensure the success of your project. With these practices in place, you’ll be well-equipped to tackle complex scientific challenges while maintaining reproducibility and efficiency.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
In this post I am going to give a brief introduction to one of the central ideas in theoretical physics. quantum field theory might seem a daunting subject, but behind the intimidating mathematical formulation lies an approachable interpretation for describing physics processes. Like most physicists, I was first taught field theory in the form of canonical quantization. However, I find the alternative approach of the path integral formalism to much more approachable and intuitive. Path integral formulations also exist for statistical mechanics applications, but here I will describe how it is used in quantum mechanics.
Initially, quantum field theory grew out of an attempt to reconcile special relativity with Quantum Mechanics. While Quantum Mechanics describes quantum states and their evolution and interaction, central to Quantum Field Theory are the fields whose behavior are described by the Lagrangian and the Euler-Lagrange field equations. These fields then act on states, possibly creating and annihilating quanta (or particles) of the field. Using the path integral of the field it is possible to calculate probabilities for processes that can be observed. Quantum field theories are able to explain particle interaction and the creation and annihilation of particles that does not occur in standard quantum mechanics making such theories much more flexible. The Standard Model is built in terms of quantum field theories, where each fundamental particle is described by a field.
There are plenty of good resources for learning about quantum field theory and path integrals, but I will rely heavily on the book by Zee (2010). It is an excellent introduction to the subject and I highly recommend it.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
Path Integrals in Quantum Mechanics
The underlying principle of the path integral approach is that all possible paths of evolution from the initial to final state are considered. When a quantum state evolves from one state to another, we consider and incorporate all contributions from all possible paths into a final amplitude that describes the process. The advantage of the path integral method in quantum mechanical calculations is that it provides a simpler method of calculating certain processes, and in particular it gives a much more elegant way of approaching field theory. I will start by following MacKenzie (2000). The path integral determines the amplitude of evolving from one state to another. Quantum mechanically, the amplitude for this is
\[
M=\bra{q'}e^{-iHT}\ket{q}.
\]
Where I have used the notation \(\bra{q'}\) to signify the state at time \(T\) and \(\ket{q}\) to signify the state at time \(0\). The Hamiltonian \(H\) is the operator that governs the evolution of the system. The amplitude \(M\) is a complex number that gives the probability of evolving from state \(\ket{q}\) to state \(\bra{q'}\) in time \(T\). Now the aim is to derive this amplitude as a sum over histories of all paths between q and q’. This is done by separating the time period into a small \(\delta t=T/N\).
\[
M=\bra{q'}e^{-iH\delta t}e^{-iH\delta t}e^{-iH\delta t}...e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{q}
\]
Then the intervening states are included by using the completeness condition
\[
1=\int\ket{q}\bra{q}dq
\]
so it is possible to write
\[
M=\int dq_1dq_2..dq_{N-1} \bra{q'}e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{q_{N-1}}\bra{q_{N-1}}e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{q_{N-2}}\\
\bra{q_{N-2}}e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{q_{N-3}}...\bra{q_1}e^{-iH\delta t}\ket{q}
\]
which is just a sum over a product of all possible possibilities. This is reminiscent of the double slit experiment in which light is fed through two slits. If there are two slits (Figure 1), there are two possible paths, and two corresponding factors, but as extra slits are added the number increases.








one barrier







two barriers







three barriers






Figure 1: The double slit experiment with one, two and three barriers. The number of paths increases with the number of barriers.



We can extend the analogy of barriers in a double slit experiment to time steps in an evolution from one state to another. Now that the time steps are small, the exponents in the individual factors can be expanded using a Taylor series and taken to first order. Taking one of the factors
\[
M_{j,j+1}=\braket{q_{j+1} | q_j}-i\delta t\bra{q_{j+1}}H\ket{q_j}+O(\delta t^2).
\]
And using the completeness relation in momentum space \(\int\dfrac{dp}{2\pi}\ket{p}\bra{p}=1\) we can retrieve
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_{j,j+1}&=\braket{q_{j+1} | q_j}-i\delta t\bra{q_{j+1}}H\int\dfrac{dp_j}{2\pi}\ket{p_j}\braket{p_j |q_j}\\
&=\int\dfrac{dp_j}{2\pi} e^{ip_j (q_{j+1}-q_j)}e^{-i\delta t H}\\
&=\int\dfrac{dp_j}{2\pi} e^{i\delta t( p_j \dot{q_j}- H)}
\end{aligned}
\]
When this is taken over all the factors j up to N then the total propagator is
\[
M=\int \prod_{j=1}^{N-1}dq_j \int\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}\dfrac{dp_j}{2\pi} \exp{ i\delta t\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}.
( p_j \dot{q_j}- H)}
\]
Now let N tend to infinity so there are an infinite number of paths. This gives the phase-space integral
\[
M=\int Dp Dq \exp{(iS)}.
\]
Which can be transformed into the configuration space path integral by performing the integral over the momenta
\[
\begin{aligned}
M &=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} \left(\frac{-im}{2\pi \delta t}  \right)^{N/2} \left( \prod_{j=1}^{N-1}\int dq_j\right) e^{iS}\\
M &=\int Dq e^{iS}
\end{aligned}
\]
Where the definition of the Hamiltonian has been used to replace the factor in the exponent with the Lagrangian and then the action.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
section: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
To move from quantum mechanics the quantum field theory, only a small change is needed to the path integral. In quantum field theory the states are no longer the basic objects; they are replaced by fields that act on vacuum states to create particles.
It is now the Lagrangian density that appears in the action. The Lagrangian density is a function of the field and its derivatives rather than the position and momentum of a particle as in the quantum mechanical case. The variable q in the path integral is replaced by the field \(\phi\), the index j becomes a continuum and the path integral is no longer taken as the evolution between two states \(\ket{q},\ket{q'}\) but between two vacuum states, \(\ket{0}\). This is only convention and represents the fact it is possible to create any state by acting the field operator on the vacuum. So the path integral becomes
\[
Z=\int D\phi e^{i\int \mathcal{L}d^4 x}
\]
The question now with the path integral in quantum field theory is how to use it to find observables. The key component one can find from the path integral is the propagator, which gives the probability of a particle moving from one point to another. The propagator is derived from the action and is a central object in quantum field theory.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
The Propagator
The square of the absolute value of the propagator gives us the probability of a particle moving from one place to another (hence propagation) and is derived from the governing equation of the field. The path integral for a scalar field theory is (lower case letters like x, y signify 4-vectors)
\[
Z=\int D\phi e^{iS}
\]
where D signifies the integration measure that includes the product, limit etc. S is the action given by
\[
S=\int d^4 x \dfrac{1}{2} (\partial_\mu \phi \partial^\mu \phi -m^2\phi^2)+J\phi.
\]
Where J is some source function and \(\mu \in(0,1,2,3,4)\). To calculate the propagator first one must focus on the action and integrate by parts to get
\[
\int d^4 x \left[ -\phi\frac{1}{2}(\partial_\mu \partial^\mu +m^2)\phi +J\phi\right].
\]
Then use the Green’s function form
\[
(\partial_\mu \partial^\mu +m^2)D(x-y)=-\delta^{(4)}(x-y)
\]
such that the field satisfies
\[
\phi(x)=\int d^4 y D(x-y)J(y)
\]
and putting this form into the action above, the result is
\[
\frac{1}{2}\int d^4 x \int d^4 y J(x) D(x-y) J(y)
\]
and using Fourier transforms shows the explicit appearance of the propagator
\[
\tilde{D}(k)=\dfrac{1}{k^2-m^2}
\]
where the denominator can be replaced by whatever dispersion relation that follows the simple scalar field in Minkowski space form i.e just add extra positive terms for time-like dimensions and negative ones for space-like dimensions.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
The Potential
A simple application of the propagator is to calculate the potential between two particles. The potential is a measure of the interaction between particles and can be derived from the propagator. In quantum field theory, the potential is not a fundamental quantity but rather an emergent one that arises from the interactions of particles. The potential can be found by taking the spatial Fourier transform of the propagator. The hardest and perhaps most important part is how the sources and sinks are set up in the calculation of a potential. In the path integral formulation this must be done to allow a potential to appear, after all there can be no propagator and hence no potential without anything to propagate between.
As a first example the potential will derived in 3+1 dimensions using a source function that consists of two Dirac delta sources \(J(x)=\delta^{(3)}(\vec{x}-\vec{x_1})+ \delta^{(3)}(\vec{x}-\vec{x_2})\). These are fixed at the spatial positions \(\vec{x_1}\) and \(\vec{x_2}\). There will be a number of terms in the action arising from the product of the two source functions but since the only interesting one is where a particle is created at 1 and annihilated at 2 the only one that is considered is
\[
S=-\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^4} \int d^4 x' \int d^4 x \int d^4 k \dfrac{\delta(\vec{x}-\vec{x_1}) e^{ik\cdot(x-x')} \delta(\vec{x'}-\vec{x'_2})}{\omega^2-k^2-m^2}
\]
Where the sources are placed at a particular position in space but have no fixed time coordinate. This leads to
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=-\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^4} \int dt' \int dt \int d\omega e^{i\omega(t-t')} \int d^3 k \dfrac{e^{-i\vec{k}(\vec{x_1}-\vec{x'_2})}}{\omega^2-k^2-m^2}\\
&=-\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^3}\int dt \int d\omega \delta(\omega) \int d^3 k \dfrac{e^{-i\vec{k}(\vec{x_1}-\vec{x'_2})}}{\omega^2-k^2-m^2}\\
&=\dfrac{1}{(2\pi)^3}\int dt \int d^3 k \dfrac{e^{i\vec{k}(\vec{x_1}-\vec{x'_2})}}{k^2+m^2}
\end{aligned}
\]
Letting the time integral be \(\int dt=T\) to make the association with the T in \(\bra{0} e^{-iHT}\ket{0}=e^{-iET}\) so the potential is (and writing \(\vec{x}=\vec{x_1}-\vec{x'_2}\))
\[
\int \dfrac{d^3 k}{(2\pi)^3}\dfrac{e^{i\vec{k}.\vec{x}}}{k^2+m^2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi r}e^{-mr}
\]
Another important point is the validity of fixing the source and sink in space but not in time. When this was done is was clear that a Dirac delta function appeared in \(\omega\) that cut out the time-term from the propagator. From the path integral approach as described in Zee (2010) the specification of the sources and sinks is essential to correctly calculate the potential arising from particle propagation from source to sink.
This form of potential between two particles is called the Yukawa potential. It acts as the familiar Coulomb potential for massless particles, but for massive particles the potential is exponentially suppressed at large distances.

title: Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory
text:
Conclusion
In this brief intro I have mentioned some high-level concepts such as Green’s functions, four-vectors and the Lagrangian density. These are all important concepts in quantum field theory and this post shouldn’t be seen as a comprehensive guide, but rather a jumping off point to explore these ideas further. The path integral approach to quantum field theory is a powerful tool that allows for the calculation of probabilities and potentials in a way that is I think is more intuitive than the canonical quantization approach. It is a central part of the modern understanding of particle physics and is essential for understanding the Standard Model.

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
Particle colliders investigate the fundamental structure of matter using collisions of particles at high energies. These collisions produce jets of particles that spray out into the detector, and the structure of these jets is determined by the interactions of the particles involved. The physics of jets and their production is of particular importance in hadron colliders like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, where protons are collided at very high energies.
This post will cover an advanced treatment of the field theory for understanding these collisions, where we calculate the cross-section for the collision and its angular profile. Because the LHC collides protons, which are made of quarks and gluons, the strong force mediates the interaction; we must therefore use quantum chromodynamics (QCD) to describe the interactions.
This post is a write-up of some notes of quantum chromodynamics I made some time ago, but will put up now. The core Phenomenology. Phenomenology is the study of the interactions of particles and their decays, with a focus on drawing out measurable and experimentally-relevant results. In this case we will be looking at the decay of a photon into a quark-antiquark pair and the subsequent emission of gluons from the quarks. In the end we will find the matrix elements for these processes and to study the angular ordering that results from the collinear limit. It will be very mathematical; the aim is to show some calculations as is. These derive from quantum field theory, gauge theories and the standard model of particle physics. The results are useful for understanding the structure of jets in hadron colliders like the LHC and phenomena like the running of the strong coupling constant.
For a clear introduction to quantum field theory and the QCD requirred for this post, I recommend the following books. The standard reference for quantum field theory is Peskin (2018), but I also recommend Thomson (2013) as an accessible source for particle physics in general. For QCD in particular, the lecture notes by Mangano (1999) and Skands (2013) are excellent resources. For extra information about the running of the strong coupling constant and quark confinement, consider these notes by Deur, Brodsky, and Téramond (2016).

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
Assumptions
We start with certain assumptions that greatly simplify the calculations and enable us to produce much simpler expressions for the matrix elements.These are:

Softness of the emitted gluons with respect to the quarks. This means that for gluon 4-momentum k and quark/antiquark 4-momenta \(P_1, P_2\); \(k<<P_1,P_2\) and we can neglect any terms quadratic in k.
Massless quarks. The momenta involved in the interaction are such that the masses are negligible and can be neglected. This assumption also allows us to simplify our calculations further by using the Dirac equations \(\bar{u}(p_1)\not{p_1}=0, \not{p_2}v(p_2)=0\)
Collinearity. The gluon momenta are at small angles from the quark momenta and the decay products are at small angles to each other.

Note the use ‘dashed’ notation for 4-momenta, e.g. \(p_1\) is the 4-momentum of the first fermion in the decay and \(\not{p_1}=\gamma^\mu p_{1\mu}\) is the Dirac operator acting on that momentum. The Dirac spinors \(u(p)\) and \(v(p)\) are used to represent fermions and antifermions respectively.

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
One Photon Emission
With one soft photon emission \(\gamma \rightarrow q \bar{q}+\gamma\) we have two diagrams. From assumption (2) we have neglected the masses in the propagators. The diagrams for this decay follow the form in Figure 5






Figure 5: The decay with one photon emission. The original photon has decayed into a electron-positron pair, one of which then proceeds to emit a low-energy soft photon.



\[
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie\gamma^\mu\left[ -i\frac{\not{p_2}+\not{k}}{(p_2+k)^2}\epsilon_\nu (k) ie\gamma^\nu + \epsilon_\nu (k) ie\gamma^\nu i\frac{\not{p_1}+\not{k}}{(p_1+k)^2}\right]v(p_2)
\]
This expression is equivalent to the element in Equation 1, but with an additional expression (in square brackets) that represents the contrubtion from the photon emission. When we apply assumption (1) such that \((p_2+k)^2=p_2^2+k^2+2p_2.k=2p_2.k\) and the general expression \(\not{p}\not{k}+\not{k}\not{p}=2p.k\) and remembering that \(\epsilon_\mu \gamma^\mu=\not{\epsilon}\) and finally using the Dirac equations specified in assumption (2) we can then find:
\[
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie^2 \gamma^\mu v(p_2)\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\]
and when we compare with Equation 1 we can then write:
\[
M_{e^+e^-\gamma}=M_{e^+e^-}e\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\]
\[
\begin{align*}
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2 &=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \sum\limits_{i} \epsilon_\mu^i \epsilon_\nu^{* i} \left[\frac{p_1^\mu}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2^\mu}{p_2.k}\right]\left[\frac{p_1^\nu}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2^\nu}{p_2.k}\right]\\
&=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
$\end{align*}
\]
\[
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2=e^2\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
\tag{2}\]
Where we have used the sum over photon polarizations \(\sum\limits_{i} \epsilon_\mu^i \epsilon_\nu^{* i}=-g_{\mu \nu}\) and we neglect terms like \(p_1.p_1\) or \(p_2.p_2\). This is the squared matrix element for the decay of a photon into an electron-positron pair with one soft photon emission. This expression can be directly incorporated into the cross-section for the decay and is used to calculate the angular distribution of the emitted photon in a collider.

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
Two Photon Emission
Two photon emission proceeds in the say way as with one photon. We have 4 possible diagrams this time and so four terms in the amplitude. These correspond to the two photons being emitted from the electron or the positron, and the order of emission. The first two diagrams are where the first photon is emitted from the electron and the second from the positron (Figure 6) and vice versa. The second two diagrams are where both photons are emitted from the positron (Figure 7) or vice versa. The momenta in this case satisfy \(q=p_1+p_2+k_a+k_b\) with \(k_a,k_b<<p_1,p_2\). In the two photon emission the softer photon is always emitted second, as it cannot be emitted from a more off-shell line. This also holds true for gluons and shall be used later. The first diagram component to the amplitude is:






Figure 6: The first two photon emission diagram. There are three vertex factors for this diagram, corresponding to the initial photon decay, followed by the subsequent photon emissions respectively.



\[
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma} &=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\nu \epsilon_\nu(k_a) i\frac{(\not{p_1}+\not{k_a})}{(p_1+k_a)^2} ie\gamma^\mu(-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\rho \epsilon_\rho(k_b)v(p_2)\\
&=-\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
\]
For the second diagram we can simply do \(p_1 \Leftrightarrow p_2\) so that we get
\[
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}=-\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
\]






Figure 7: The diagram for the matrix element for two photon emission from the positron.



For the other two diagrams:
\[
\begin{align*}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_a+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\nu \epsilon_\nu(k_a) (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_b)^2} ie\gamma^\rho \epsilon_\rho(k_b)v(p_2)\\
&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}v(p_2)
\end{align*}
\]
And again reversing the quark momenta
\[
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie \gamma^\mu \frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}v(p_2)
\]
Collecting all these together we get
\[
\begin{align}
M_{e^+e^-\gamma\gamma}&=M_{e^+e^-}e^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}+\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}\right]\\
&=M_{e^+e^-}e^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\right]\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}\right]
\end{align}
\tag{3}\]
When we square this with the methods used to obtain Equation 2 we arrive at
\[
\vert M_{e^+e^-\gamma}\vert^2=e^4\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_a p_2.k_a}\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_b p_2.k_b}
\]
As we can see in Equation 3 the number of terms in the matrix element is just the number of possible diagrams and the terms themselves are products of n factors like \(\frac{p.\epsilon}{p.k}\) for n photons emitted. When we square the matrix element we find that for n emitted photons the squared matrix element is always of the form:
\[
\vert M_{e^+e^- n\gamma}\vert^2=\vert M_{e^+e^-}\vert^2 \prod\limits_{i}^n W_i
\tag{4}\]
Where the \(W_i\) are factors of the form \(\frac{p_i.\epsilon}{p_i.k}\) for each emitted photon. This is a very useful result as it allows us to write the squared matrix element for any number of photons emitted from a fermion pair in terms of the original matrix element for the fermion pair decay. Where I define the W as
\[
W_1:=g^2\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_i p_2.k_i}
\tag{5}\]
Expression Equation 4 will reappear when we look at gluon emissions.

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
Coherence
We now apply the collinearity assumption. This is that the the decay products (in the case of QED above it is an electron/positron pair) are at small angles and the emitted bosons are also at small angles. In the QED matrix element we have the W factor defined in Equation 5 and if we remember that \(p.k=E_p E_k-E_p E_k cos\theta_{pk}\). Since in this limit and using natural units we write \(E=p\). This then implies that for the W factor we get.
\[
g^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}=\frac{g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{2(1-cos \theta_{12})}{(1-cos \theta_{1k})(1-cos \theta_{2k})}
\tag{6}\]
Since also \(E_k= \omega_k\) in natural units. The angle \(\theta_{12}\) is the angle between the two fermions, \(\theta_{1k}\) is the angle between fermion 1 and the photon k. This notation shall be used for the rest of this post with the fermions as numbers and the bosons as latin letters. As we are using the collinear assumption, we can replace the cosine with the first couple of terms in its Taylor series expansion. and so Equation 6 then becomes:
\[
\frac{g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{2(1-cos \theta_{12})}{(1-cos \theta_{1k})(1-cos \theta_{2k})}\simeq \frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{\theta_{12}^2}{\theta_{1k}^2 \theta_{2k}^2}
\tag{7}\]
Here we now have two cases, one where \(\theta_{1k}\) or \(\theta_{2k}<<\theta_{12}\) i.e the boson is close in angle to one of the fermions in which case the expression above simplifies slightly, or we have \(\theta_{12}<<\theta_{1k}\simeq \theta_{2k}\) where the emitted boson is far away in angle. This latter case is coherence and the photon radiation is suppressed as we do not see the charges of the fermion pair. This means that the former case is of importance to us but not the latter. So we can now write Equation 7 as a sum of the two cases where the boson is emitted close to one or the other using a step function \(\Theta\).
\[
\frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{\theta_{12}^2}{\theta_{1k}^2 \theta_{2k}^2}\simeq \frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{1}{\theta_{1k}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{1k})+\frac{4g^2}{\omega^2_k}\frac{1}{\theta_{2k}^2} \Theta(\theta_{12}-\theta_{2k})
\tag{8}\]
This is angular ordering and shall be applied to QCD.

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
One Gluon Emission
One gluon emission proceeds like that of the one photon emission, since with only one boson we don’t get any correlated emission. Differences however arise from the gluon vertex factor and the Gell-Mann matrix (\(t^a\)) it contains. We consider the decay \(\gamma\rightarrow q \bar{q}+g\). With diagrams of the form in Figure 8.






Figure 8: The decay to a quark-antiquark pair with a single gluon emission off the anitquark



In this case the matrix element is
\[
\begin{align}
M_{q\bar{q}g}&=\epsilon_\mu (q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie g_s \gamma^\mu v(p_2)t^a\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s t^a\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon}{p_1.k}- \frac{p_2.\epsilon}{p_2.k}\right]
\end{align}  
\]
When we square the element we must use the sum \(\sum\limits_a t^a t^a=C_f=4/3\), which comes from the trace of the Gell-Mann matrices. This gives us the squared matrix element for one gluon emission:
\[
\vert M_{q\bar{q}g}\vert^2=C_fg_s^2\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k p_2.k}
\]
We can see that this differs from the QED case only by the constants \(e^2\Rightarrow C_f g_s^2\)

title: Gluons in colliders
text:
Two Gluon Emission
For two gluon emission we have six diagrams and the prospect of correlated emission. This effect leads to the matrix element for the gluon case changing drastically from the much simpler two photon emission in Equation 3 . Four of our six diagrams are independent emission diagrams and so are the same as the four diagrams of the two photon emission with the addition of Gell-Mann matrices from the quark-gluon vertex. So without the correlated emission our matrix element is:
\[
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s^2\left[t^bt^a\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}+t^at^b\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-t^at^b\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-t^bt^a\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}\right]
\]






Figure 9: The independent emission diagram for two gluons. There is a corresponding diagram for dual independent emission from the quark.









Figure 10: One of the two correlated emission diagrams. The gluon-gluon coupling sees the triple-gluon vertex appear in this decay.



The last two matrix elements come from the correlated emission of two gluons where we have a triple gluon vertex, illustrated in Figure 10. Note we also make use of the structure constant \(f^{abc}\) of the Gell-Mann matrices, which is defined by the commutation relation \([t^a,t^b]= i f^{abc} t^c\). The matrix element for these two diagrams is:
\[
\begin{align*}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=\epsilon_\mu(q)\bar{u}(p_1)ie\gamma^\mu (-i)\frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a}+\not{k_b})}{(p_2+k_a+k_b)^2} i g_s\gamma^\nu t^d\frac{(-ig_{\nu\rho}\delta^{dc})}{(k_a+k_b)^2}(-1)g_s f^{abc}\\\left[g^{\rho\beta}(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +g^{\beta\gamma}(-k_a+k_b)^\rho +g^{\gamma\rho} (-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a) \epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)v(p_2)
\end{align*}
\]
We apply the ‘second gluon is softer’ condition so that we can ignore \(k_b\) in the propagator and applying the other assumptions we get
\[
\begin{align*}
M_{q\bar{q}gg}&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a})}{2p_2.k_a}\frac{\gamma^\nu g_{\nu\rho}}{2k_a.k_b}\\
&\left[\epsilon^{\rho*}(k_a)\epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +\epsilon_a.\epsilon_b(-k_a+k_b)^\rho +\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a) \epsilon^{\rho*} (k_b)(-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{(\not{p_2}+\not{k_a})}{2p_2.k_a}\frac{1}{2k_a.k_b}\left[\not{\epsilon_a}\epsilon_\gamma^* (k_b)(2k_a+k_b)^\gamma +\not{\epsilon_b}\epsilon_\beta^*(k_a)(-2k_b-k_a)^\beta \right]\\
&=M_{q\bar{q}} i f^{abc}g_s^2 t^c \frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b}
\end{align*}
\]
We have ignored the term involving \(\epsilon_a.\epsilon_b\) since it becomes like \(\not{k}\) which we have neglected. The last component to the matrix element is found by the substitution \(p_1\Leftrightarrow p_2\) into the equation above. When we include all the components we find the total matrix element is
\[
M_{q\bar{q}gg}=M_{q\bar{q}}g_s^2\left[\frac{p_1.\epsilon_a}{p_1.k_a}-\frac{p_2.\epsilon_a}{p_2.k_a}\right]\left[t^bt^a \frac{p_1.\epsilon_b}{p_1.k_b}-t^a t^b\frac{p_2.\epsilon_b}{p_2.k_b}-i f^{abc}t^c \frac{k_a.\epsilon_b}{k_a.k_b} \right]
\tag{9}\]
To square the element, we must sum over the different colour states of the gluons
\[
\begin{align*}
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2&=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2 \frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_a p_2.k_a}[\sum\limits_{col}\frac{2p_1.p_2}{p_1.k_b p_2.k_b}t^a t^b t^a t^b +\\
&\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b} i f^{abc} (t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)-\frac{p_1.k_a}{p_1.k_b k_a.k_b}if^{abc} (t^c t^a t^b - t^b t^a t^c)]\\
&=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2[\frac{W_a}{N_c} 2 W_b Tr(t^a t^b t^a t^b)+\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b} i f^{abc} Tr(t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)\\
&-\frac{p_1.k_a}{p_1.k_b k_a.k_b}if^{abc} Tr(t^c t^a t^b - t^b t^a t^c)]
\end{align*}
\]
I have used the W defined in Equation 5 and now we can use some relations to simplify this result
\[
\begin{align*}
t^a t^b t^a&=-\frac{t^b}{2N_c}\Rightarrow Tr(t^a t^b t^a t^b)=-\frac{Tr(t^b t^b)}{2N_c}=-C_f/2\\
&[t^a,t^b]=i f^{abc} t^c\Rightarrow i f^{abc} Tr(t^c t^b t^a-t^a t^b t^c)=f^{abc}f^{abd} Tr(t^c t^d)=C_a Tr(t^c t^c)=C_a^2 C_f
\end{align*}
\]
\(C_a=N_c\) and the above can simplify the squared amplitude to
\[
\vert M_{q\bar{q}gg}\vert^2=g_s^4\vert M_{q\bar{q}}\vert^2  W_a C_f \left[N_c\frac{p_2.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_2.k_b}+N_c \frac{p_1.k_a}{k_a.k_b p_1.k_b}- \frac{1}{N_c}W_b\right]
\tag{10}\]

title: SQL Notes
text:
Access and manipulate relational databases. These organise data into tables. Each datum has a type, usually INTEGER, TEXT, DATE, REAL, NULL
We run queries against the database. Usually in a script.sqlite file
Creation/manipulation keywords
Query Keywords
Multi-table commands

title: SQL Notes
text:
Syntax & creating/manipulating tables
statements end with semi-colon
We create tables with CREATE
CREATE TABLE celebs (
  id INTEGER,
  name TEXT,
  age INTEGER
 );
create a table with column names and their type
We add data to the table with INSERT
INSERT INTO celebs (id, name, age) 
VALUES (1, 'Justin Bieber', 29);
We select data from a table with SELECT
SELECT name FROM celebs;
We can change a table with the ALTER command, here we add a new column
ALTER TABLE celebs 
ADD COLUMN twitter_handle TEXT;
We can edit rows using the UPDATE statement, here we update the table celebs at locations defined by WHERE
UPDATE celebs 
SET twitter_handle = '@taylorswift13' 
WHERE id = 4; 
We can remove data with the DELETE statement
DELETE FROM celebs 
WHERE twitter_handle IS NULL;
Constraints that add information about how a column can be used are invoked after specifying the data type for a column. They can be used to tell the database to reject inserted data that does not adhere to a certain restriction. Here we define constraints on columns so that there is

PRIMARY KEY so that this row is unique and any rows with duplicate ids are rejected
UNIQUE columns are those where each row in the column for forced to be unique
NOT NULL ensures data with NULL values rejected in insertion
DEFAULT ensures rows have a default value if new data does not specify value

CREATE TABLE celebs (
   id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, 
   name TEXT UNIQUE,
   date_of_birth TEXT NOT NULL,
   date_of_death TEXT DEFAULT 'Not Applicable'
);
Using these basic statements we can create tables, add data, remove data and manipulate tables in a way subject to contraints

title: SQL Notes
text:
Querying a database
We select particular columns
SELECT column1, column2 
FROM table_name;
We can select columns under an alias using the AS keyword
SELECT name AS 'Titles'
FROM movies;
The DISTICT keyword can be used to find all the unique values of a column
SELECT DISTINCT tools 
FROM inventory;
We can extract data according to conditions using the WHERE keyword and boolean operators
SELECT *
FROM movies
WHERE imdb_rating > 8;
Standard operators operators are AND, OR, NOT alongside = > < <= != >=
We can use the LIKE keyword to apply regex or wildcard style filters to the data
SELECT * 
FROM movies
WHERE name LIKE 'Se_en';
Useful wildcards are ’_’ ‘%’
SELECT * 
FROM movies 
WHERE name LIKE '%man%';
We identify NULL values not by using = or != but rather with IS NULL IS NOT NULL
We can select date in a range using the BETWEEN keyword. This works with numbers (INTERGER, REAL, FLOAT), dates and TEXT.
We can create complex conditions by combining operators and boolean operators AND OR NOT
SELECT * 
FROM movies
WHERE year BETWEEN 1990 AND 1999
   AND genre = 'romance';
We can sort the resulting query using the ORDER BY keyword (ASC, DESC can be used to get ascending or deceasing order)
SELECT name, year
FROM movies
ORDER BY name DESC;
We can limit the size of the resulting output with the LIMIT keyword - useful for very big tables
SELECT * FROM movies
ORDER BY imdb_rating DESC
LIMIT 3
The CASE keyword allows us to perform if/then logic, possibly returning the result under an alias. Here we select name and a new revew column that maps values of the rating column into a new review column based on if/then logic (WHEN/THEN)
SELECT name,
 CASE
  WHEN imdb_rating > 8 THEN 'Fantastic'
  WHEN imdb_rating > 6 THEN 'Poorly Received'
  ELSE 'Avoid at All Costs'
 END AS 'Review'
FROM movies;

title: SQL Notes
text:
Aggregation
We can apply standard aggregation functions like

COUNT
SUM
MAX
MIN
AVG
ROUND

Count the number of rows in a table, possibly with optional selection logic
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM table_name;
Sum the values of a particular column
SELECT SUM(downloads)
FROM fake_apps;
MIN/MAX/AVG work in a similar way
Rounding is performed by specifiying the column and number of decimal places
SELECT name, ROUND(price, 0)
FROM fake_apps;

title: SQL Notes
text:
Group by
Group by can be used with aggregation functions to arrage identical data into groups before performing an operation. For example, we can find the average rating grouped by each year.
SELECT year,
   AVG(imdb_rating)
FROM movies
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year;
We can group by a result of a calculation, and we can also refer to selected columns using indices e.g
SELECT ROUND(imdb_rating),
   COUNT(name)
FROM movies
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
It is possible to do a double group by. Here we find the average downloads for each categrory and price level
SELECT category, 
   price,
   AVG(downloads)
FROM fake_apps
GROUP BY 1, 2;
We can filter groups by using the HAVING keyword - it acts as a filter for groups, whereas WHERE acted as a filter for rows
SELECT category, 
   price,
   AVG(downloads)
FROM fake_apps
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING AVG(downloads) > 10;

title: SQL Notes
text:
Multi tables
We can split our data across multiple tables in the database, while maintaining the ability to cross-reference the data across tables. We look at data across tables by joining two or more tables. This is done with the JOIN keyword. This performs an inner join, only connecting values that exist in both.
SELECT *
FROM orders
JOIN subscriptions
  ON orders.subscription_id = subscriptions.subscription_id;
Here we selected all columns and joined the two tables absed on the subscription_id column. We could run further selection logic with WHERE or GROUP BY etc.
We perform a left join where we keep all the rows of the left table. We can also as usual perform some selection/group logic on the results.
SELECT *
FROM table1
LEFT JOIN table2
  ON table1.c2 = table2.c2;
SELECT month,
  COUNT(*)
FROM newspaper
CROSS JOIN months
WHERE start_month <=month AND end_month>=month
GROUP BY month;
Here we cross-joined newspaper subscriber info on months, the counted the number of monthly subscribers using groupby
We can wholesale join two tables together using UNION
SELECT *
FROM newspaper
UNION
SELECT *
FROM online;
We can join a table to the result of a calculation query using the WITH keyword. This essentially creates a temporary table from a calculation result, with which we can join to our other table/
WITH previous_results AS (
   SELECT ...
   ...
   ...
   ...
)
SELECT *
FROM previous_results
JOIN customers
  ON _____ = _____;
Here we create a temporary previous_query table and join it to the customers table based on the id
WITH previous_query AS (
SELECT customer_id,
   COUNT(subscription_id) AS 'subscriptions'
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customers.customer_name, previous_query.subscriptions
FROM customers
JOIN previous_query
  ON customers.customer_id = previous_query.customer_id;

Using a SQLite database
In SQLite, a database is stored in a single file — a trait that distinguishes it from other database engines. This fact allows for a great deal of accessibility: copying a database is no more complicated than copying the file that stores the data, sharing a database can mean sending an email attachment. It is most useful if you don’t need to use a server - where everything is local
SQLite does not enforce schema, so datatypes can be wrong and contraints will not be enforced
This works via a CLI sqlite3, e.g. sqlite3 newdb.sqlite
Create a new local database sqlite3 new.db
Export to a file by ‘.output filename.txt’
Run scripts with ‘.read script.sql’, this will run the commands in the script as a normal interpreter
Import data from a file with ‘.import –csv –schema schema-name file.csv table_1’
Export
sqlite3 -header -csv your_database.db "SELECT * FROM your_table;" > filename.csv
Import
sqlite3 your_database.db ".mode csv" ".import /path/to/your_file.csv table_name"
Run scripts
sqlite3 your_database.db < /path/to/your_script.sql
creation sqlite3 data.db < make_db.sql
querying sqlite3 -header -table data.db < query.sql
importing csv sqlite3 data.db ".mode csv" ".import extra_data.csv wardens"
export sqlite3 -header -csv data.db "SELECT date, AVG(temperature) FROM observations GROUP BY date;" > export.csv

Development Process

Mathematics - decide on the application itself and the mathematical method it will apply
Setup repo - see package design
Setup version control
Decide if you are creating a script or library module
git branch for new feature, such as a new script or library module
Use pip install -e . to develop, run tests over the project
When a script/class is complete, profile with timeit or cProfile to optimize (optional)
Format with black and pylint.
At each complete unit of work (when a new feature has been implemented), commit the changes to the branch. Commit also when you have made changes you may want to undo.
git push at the end of the day or when the branch is merged
package and publish (if necessary)


Scripts vs. libraries vs. notebooks
When developing python scripts vs library modules, the former is for performing a particular task with well defined inputs and outputs, the latter is for creating useful classes and functions that are imported by other code. They are designed to abstract tasks and be reused frequently. The development process is very different.
Developing a library module:

create the library module
Design classes - what they will do, what are the nouns (objects) and verbs (functions) of the software, class compositions
Write documentation as you go - see documentation section
Write tests - in separate tests folder, use pytest for running them - follow the test-driven-development process
Write classes - test as you go

Develop a script:

Copy the script template
decide on the task of the script, define the desired input and output
Analysis scripts are best when modular, this means that if it is getting too large, split the analysis into separate scripts doing a particular task with well defined inputs and outputs.
The key is iteration rate, make sure there is a ‘fast’ mode, or a small input size for development and debugging before the ‘big’ run.
Debug with pdb or IDE debugger as you go

A python project can be a single script, a pure library, a library with a single “run” or “main” script or a set of scripts together with a library of common code utilities. Avoid using debugging for library modules, instead prefer a good set of unit tests. Scripts are the reverse, rely on a debugger. You shouldn’t need a lot of unit tests for the components of a script, if you do, this is a sign that function or class might be better added to a library of utilities and covered by unit tests.
Developing a notebook
The purpose of a notebook is interactive, procedural analysis. Usually this will be in jupyter notebooks but I prefer using pycharm’s code cells and standard python scripts.

These do not have the standard main function
No arguments, and not run on the command line
do retain the rest of the structure of a script

title: Python Notes
text:
Testing & debugging

test-driven development

requirements are turned into very specific test cases, then the code is improved so that the tests pass. A unit test checks the output of a small component of the whole application. One can write unit and integration tests with the help of the pytest and unittest libraries.
It helps to install a editable version using pip install -e . this will allow you to change the code, while running tests.

Unit tests

pytest unit tests

The key keyword is the assert term. This term will take in a boolean argument but only raise an error if the argument is false. It is used in unit test functions like so
def test_sum():
    assert sum([1, 2, 3]) == 6, "Should be 6"

There will usually be a test function like test_sum for each function or class (in the case of classes, the class is instantiated and all methods are tested within one test_class function).
One can combine pytest and debugging with the --pdb flag, which opens pdb on errors found by pytest
One can benchmark a test with pytest-benchmark to log the timing of each test case. This tells us the time of execution as well as evaluation

def test_my_function(benchmark):
    result = benchmark(test)

Fixtures are a way of providing data, test doubles, or state setup to your tests. Fixtures are great for extracting data or objects that you use across multiple tests.

@pytest.fixture
def example_people_data():
    return [
        {
            "given_name": "Alfonsa",
            "family_name": "Ruiz",
            "title": "Senior Software Engineer",
        },
        {
            "given_name": "Sayid",
            "family_name": "Khan",
            "title": "Project Manager",
        },
    ]

def test_format_data_for_display(example_people_data):
    assert format_data_for_display(example_people_data) == [
        "Alfonsa Ruiz: Senior Software Engineer",
        "Sayid Khan: Project Manager",
    ]

def test_format_data_for_excel(example_people_data):
    assert format_data_for_excel(example_people_data) == """given,family,title
Alfonsa,Ruiz,Senior Software Engineer
Sayid,Khan,Project Manager
"""

You can run specific tests with :: pytest test_file.py::test_func_name
Parametrization is used to combine the multiple test cases into one test case.

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“num”, “result”, [(1, 11), (2,22), (3,33), (4,44), (5,55)]
def test_calculation(num, result):
  assert 11*num == result

Use the --durations option to the pytest command to include a duration report in your test results. --durations expects an integer value n and will report the slowest n number of tests. pytest --durations=3
You can group tests into a larger test class

# content of test_class.py
class TestClass:
    def test_one(self):
        x = "this"
        assert "h" in x

    def test_two(self):
        x = "hello"
        assert hasattr(x, "check")

unittest testing

Using unittset requires putting each test into a class and using assertEqual, assertFalse, assertTrue methods
import unittest


class TestSum(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_sum(self):
        self.assertEqual(sum([1, 2, 3]), 6, "Should be 6")

    def test_sum_tuple(self):
        self.assertEqual(sum((1, 2, 2)), 6, "Should be 6")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Coverage

Code coverage is the proportion of your code covered by tests. A useful tool is coverage
coverage run -m pytest arg1 arg2
Coverage can also be performed with pytest-cov which unifies pytest and coverage.


Debugging
Use the pdb module to debug python programs. use it on scripts by calling
python -m pdb script.py
then step through the lines of code with n and s or use p to print output
list source code with ll
use b to set breakpoints and use c to continue until breakpoint
debugging in IDEs
It is easy now to debug with an IDE like Pycharm. The debugging loop consists of:

open the debugger
create breakpoints
start the debugger by using “Run and debug”, selecting the script you want to debug
step through the lines of code to view variable values

The debugger is a fully functioning interpreter, so you can inspect variables, and reset others.

title: Python Notes
text:
Documentation

Docstrings
A docstring is a string that is the first statement in a package, module, class or function. These strings can be extracted automatically through the doc member of the object. A docstring should give enough information to write a call to the function without reading the function’s code.
Standard google style for function docstrings:
def fetch_bigtable_rows(big_table, keys, other_silly_variable=None):
    """Fetches rows from a Bigtable.

    Retrieves rows pertaining to the given keys from the Table instance
    represented by big_table.  Silly things may happen if
    other_silly_variable is not None.

    Args:
        big_table: An open Bigtable Table instance.
        keys: A sequence of strings representing the key of each table row
            to fetch.
        other_silly_variable: Another optional variable, that has a much
            longer name than the other args, and which does nothing.

    Returns:
        A dict mapping keys to the corresponding table row data
        fetched. Each row is represented as a tuple of strings. For
        example:

        {'Serak': ('Rigel VII', 'Preparer'),
         'Zim': ('Irk', 'Invader'),
         'Lrrr': ('Omicron Persei 8', 'Emperor')}

        If a key from the keys argument is missing from the dictionary,
        then that row was not found in the table.

    Raises:
        IOError: An error occurred accessing the bigtable.Table object.
    """
Standard google style for module docstring:
"""A one line summary of the module or program, terminated by a period.

Leave one blank line.  The rest of this docstring should contain an
overall description of the module or program.  Optionally, it may also
contain a brief description of exported classes and functions and/or usage
examples.

  Typical usage example:

  foo = ClassFoo()
  bar = foo.FunctionBar()
"""
after the module docstring you should structure your imports:
# Standard library imports
import datetime
import os

# Third party imports
from flask import Flask
from flask_restful import Api
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy

# Local application imports
from local_module import local_class
from local_package import local_function
Numpy-style docstrings
class Animal:
    """
    A class used to represent an Animal

    ...

    Attributes
    ----------
    says_str : str
        a formatted string to print out what the animal says
    name : str
        the name of the animal
    sound : str
        the sound that the animal makes
    num_legs : int
        the number of legs the animal has (default 4)

    Methods
    -------
    says(sound=None)
        Prints the animals name and what sound it makes
    """

    says_str = "A {name} says {sound}"

    def __init__(self, name, sound, num_legs=4):
        """
        Parameters
        ----------
        name : str
            The name of the animal
        sound : str
            The sound the animal makes
        num_legs : int, optional
            The number of legs the animal (default is 4)
        """

        self.name = name
        self.sound = sound
        self.num_legs = num_legs

    def says(self, sound=None):
        """Prints what the animals name is and what sound it makes.

        If the argument `sound` isn't passed in, the default Animal
        sound is used.

        Parameters
        ----------
        sound : str, optional
            The sound the animal makes (default is None)

        Raises
        ------
        NotImplementedError
            If no sound is set for the animal or passed in as a
            parameter.
        """

        if self.sound is None and sound is None:
            raise NotImplementedError("Silent Animals are not supported!")

        out_sound = self.sound if sound is None else sound
        print(self.says_str.format(name=self.name, sound=out_sound))

no need to add a description for python special methods, only define the parameters and returns
Don’t bother listing the methods in the class top docstring, just the attributes
Don’t document private methods and attributes

Auto create API documentation with pdoc
pdoc --html ./path/to/package
Using sphinx One can autogenerate api documentation from docstrings using sphinx.

create docs folder
sphinx-quickstart
create .rst files for each module with

neuroNLP.ontology
=================
.. automodule:: neuroNLP.ontology
    :members:

add sphinx.ext.autodoc and sphinx.ext.napoleon to the extensions of the conf.py
make html (or latexpdf)



Type hints
Type hints are not necessary for a dynamically typed language like python, but they do improve readability and allow static analysis to ensure you use inputs and outputs correctly. Use type checking via the mypy tool.
mypy script.py
It will look over you code and check for errors in types. For it to work you must put Rust-like type annotations into the function/class signatures
def greeting(name: str) -> str:
    return 'Hello ' + name
basic types are supported str,int,float,bool,complex, None. For compound types, import them from the typing module. from typing import <>. List,Dict,Tuple,Iterable, Union, Set, Generator. These must be defined with the data type they hold. eg. List[str], Dict[int, float], Tuple[bool]
derived types: one can create type aliases for a specific type to aid comprehension
from typing import List, Dict, Tuple

ConnectionOptions = Dict[str, str]
Address = Tuple[str, int]
Server = Tuple[Address, ConnectionOptions]
Vector = List[float]

def stringify(x: float) -> str:
    return str(x)

def summing(x: List[int]) -> int:
    ans = 0
    for i in x:
        ans += i
    return ans

def main():
    a_list = [2, 3, 4]
    summed = summing(a_list)
    stringed = stringify(4.6)
    string_list = stringify(a_list)
    print(a_list)
    print(summed)
    print(stringed)
    print(string_list)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


Pydantic
Pydantic is a data validation module that allows you to do type checking at test/runtime. It works alongside the typing library and can be a good way of avoiding all the assert/isinstance blocks.
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Tuple

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Delivery(BaseModel):
    timestamp: datetime
    dimensions: Tuple[int, int]


m = Delivery(timestamp='2020-01-02T03:04:05Z', dimensions=['10', '20'])
print(repr(m.timestamp))
#> datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, tzinfo=TzInfo(UTC))
print(m.dimensions)
#> (10, 20)

Formatting & linting
Format and lint python code to be clean, well written and conforming to a style. The best two tools are black and pylint. Also useful is isort which auto-sorts your imports. Also try ruff for faster linting
PEP8 is the python style guide. For readable, maintainable code, it is best to conform to the style guide. One can use a linter such as pylint to check for logical and stylistic errors.
format python code with black
best way to ensure style is to just run the black formatter over the whole package like black neuroNLP/
