text:
Profiling & logging
Python can be profiles with timeit
python -m timeit script.py
Python code can be profiled with cProfile. This can be used on a script like so:
python -m cProfile script.py
output a profile data file with
python -m cProfile -o script.profile script.py
then one can use pstats to analyse the profile
python -m pstats script.profile
Alternatively one can use it inside a main function like so
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # main()
    import cProfile

    cProfile.run("main()", "pipe.profile")
Python logging

useful for debugging purposes, particularly when a debugger cannot be used to step through a program.
the logging standard package provides debug, info, warning, error, critical functions to output logging info.
Normally the output is sent to stdout to the terminal, but we can also save it to a file by specifying the logging config. logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, filename="output.log")
You can customize the output format using the format keyword to config
Set the log level, and the logger will only record info over and above that level, (DEBUG-INFO-WARNING-ERROR)

import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)
logging.info("starting program")
logging.debug(f"start value is {x}")
logging.warning("warning: this is a warning")
logging.error("warning: this is a warning")

title: Python Notes
text:
Environments, modules & packaging
Each environment can use different versions of package dependencies and Python. Each project should have its own environment. They allow you to isolate each project and its dependencies.
Package - A folder/directory that contains init.py file. Module - A valid python file with .py extension.
The best tools are conda, and uv. These tools also act as package managers and module builders.

Conda
One can use different anaconda environments for different version of software to create an environment
conda create -n myenv software1 software2==2.2
conda activate myenv
To export the installed software for this environment
conda env export > environment.yml
To create an identical environment
conda env create -f environment.yml


UV
Package structure: the standard python package structure is of the form
sampleproject
├── LICENSE.txt
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── src
│   └── sample
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── package_data.dat
│       └── simple.py
├── tests
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── test_simple.py
└── tox.ini
With dependencies specified in pyproject.toml
To build a package out of several python files, make sure there is a __init__.py file in each subdirectory. This file marks each directory as a python directory and allows one to do import name.module
Other optional files are data for storing datasets, models for pre-trained models, and dev for jupyter notebooks or development scripts. If there is C-code that is compiled into a cython .so library, put the C/C++ source code and .pyx files in a src directory and compiled .so files in a lib directory.


Package distribution


Approaches to modules, packages and projects
There are two types of python project, each with a corresponding workflow and directory structure

uv: use uv for packageing and distribution https://docs.astral.sh/uv/
Scientific project: the aim is not to do software development, and not with the aim of distributing a finished, tested software tool. The aim of these projects is running particular computations, analysis and plotting rather that a well-structured python tool. For this purpose conda is enough and building/distribution is not necessary (beyond git cloning). Instead use anaconda for all environment and packaging, define dependencies with env.yaml and structure the directory thus

project
├── README.md
├── docs
│   ├── lit_rev.md
│   ├── paper_skeleton.md
│   └── plots
├── env.yaml
└── src
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── lib.py
    ├── notebook.py
    └── script.py
One can build and install with conda, via the conda-build ,conda-build skeleton commands, but you need and extra meta.yaml

title: Python Notes
text:
Language Features

Variables

The basic variable data types of python are str, int, float, complex, bool, bytes. In reality everything in python is an instance of a class. So an integer x is an instance of the int class, e.g. x = int().
Strings vs bytes: use encode and decode methods on strings and bytes to go from strings to bytes (utf-8 decoding most common). ASCII
chr, hex, bin, ord
isinstance, type



Collections
Basic collections

Both list [] and tuple () array-like index-accessed data types, however lists are mutable (you can change the elements are initialisation) but tuples are immutable (cannot change).
A set {}is a collection that holds an unordered collection of unique objects. set([1,2,3]) or {1,2,3} can also define set operations such as union s1.union(s2) or s1 | s2intersection s1.intersection(s2) or s1 & s2complement/difference s1.difference(s2) or s1 - s2
A dict {a:b} is a key-value pair mapping.

Advanced collections

namedtuple from collections is a tuple with named positions. You have to create this with a factory, where we specify the name of the tuple and field names. They are essentially python dataclasses, similar to how structs are used in C. They are immutable by default.

special_tuple = collections.namedtuple("special_tuple", "A B")
p1 = special_tuple(3,5)
p1.A
p1.B

defaultdict from collections is for when you want to have default values for dict keys. It needs to given a default function to set the default values like defaultdict(int) for 0 integer default values (could also use lambdas here). Designed to replace situations like

counter = {}
for i in "ABBDBBDA":
    if i in counter.keys():
        counter[i]+=1
    else:
        counter[i] =1

Counter from collections is a dict subclass for counting hashable objects. e.g. counting the number of unique strings in a list Counter(list_a). The update method is useful here when counting several lists Counter(list_a).update(list_b) and combining the result. Also useful is most_common. We can also add and subtract counters to combine the results of two counts. This class also supports and/not/or for checking union/complement/intersection.
OrderedDict from collections remembers order in which data was added. This means you can popitem from the top as you would a stack or iterate over the items in order as you would a list. Note for two ordereddicts to be the same the order of the data has to match as well as the items themselves.
deque from collections is a double-ended queue, a combination of a stack and a queue. you can pop from either side in a very memory efficient way. use the methods pop, popleft, append, appendleft, rotate to add and modify data.
dataclass from dataclasses reduce the boilerplate code for custom data structures with named attributes. They can create init, repr, hash and eq magic functions by default.

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Color:
    r : int = 0
    g : int = 0
    b : int = 0









Attributes
init
Color().r -> 0
init




Representation
repr
Color() -> Color(r=0, g=0, b=0)
repr


Comparision*
eq
Color() == Color(0, 0, 0) -> True
eq


Order
order
sorted([Color(0, 50, 0), Color()]) -> …
lt, le, gt, ge


Hashable
unsafe_hash/frozen
{Color(), {Color()}} -> {Color(r=0, g=0, b=0)}
hash


Immutable
frozen + eq
Color().r = 10 -> TypeError
setattr, delattr





Functions & comprehensions
def func(args):
    return result

map, reduce, filter, any, all

NOTE: prefer list comprehensions and generator expressions over map
map applies a function to all the items in an input_list. Here is the blueprint:
map(function_to_apply, list_of_inputs)
It is an iterable, so one must use the list function to get all the elements in an array.
As the name suggests, filter creates a list of elements for which a function returns true. Here is a short and concise example:
number_list = range(-5, 5)
less_than_zero = list(filter(lambda x: x < 0, number_list))
reduce is a really useful function for performing some computation on a list and returning the result. It applies a rolling computation to sequential pairs of values in a list.
from functools import reduce
product = reduce((lambda x, y: x * y), [1, 2, 3, 4])
The any function will check if any of the items in a list or iterable are true. Returns a boolean.
y = [True, False, False]
x = any(y)
The all function will check if all the items in a boolean list or tierable are true - returns a boolean
x = [True, True, True]
all(x) == True
Lambda functions

defines via func = lambda x: expression e.g. func = lambda x: x+1. Useful for short functions and functions that are passed as arguments to other functions like map, filter

Variable arguments

we can define functions that take a variable number of arguments, def function(*args): this turns a set of arguments like function(1,2,3,4,5) into a list within the function.
*args and **kwargs allow you to pass multiple arguments or keyword arguments to a function. The * is an unpacking operator that produces a tuple of positional arguments. The ** operator is similar but produces keyword arguments. That is, it produces a dictionary.

def func(*args):
   return args[0], args[3]

func(3,5,1,5,2)
#yields 3, 5
Comprehensions are ways of constructing generators or collections in a single one line.

lists [i for i in range(5)]
sets {i for i in range(5)}
dicts {i:j for i, j in enumerate('hello')}
generators (i for i in range(5))



Iterators & generators
A generator is a function that allows you to declare a function that acts like an iterator (which can be used in a for loop). An iterable object in python is built with the __next__ and __iter__ methods but a shortcut to writing iterable functions is via the yieldkeyword. When used, the function continues from when it called yield. Therefore a generator is a special type of iterator.
One can create generators using a loop and the yield keyword. The yield keyword is used in the same way as the return keyword but will instead return a generator
def generate(iterable):
    for value in iterable:
        yield value
They are particularly valuable when performing time or memory intensive computations.

the yield from keyword can be used to chain together generators
generator expressions : They function more-or-less like list comprehensions or map but avoid the overhead of generating the entire list at once. Instead, they return a generator object which can be iterated over bit-by-bit:

iterator = (s.upper() for s in oldlist)
Advanced iteration

use iter on a collection to turn it into and iterator, one can then use next to get the successive elements of the collection.
Useful when used in combination with a function and sentinel. iter(function, sentinel) The iterator will call the function successively until the output equals the sentinel value.
enumerate iterates over a collection but also returns an index as a tuple. One can also provide a starting value for the index. enumerate(collection, start=1)

When looping over an iterable and you want both the element and the number it is in the sequence, use enumerate
for i, name in enumerate(name_list):
    print(i, name)
will give you
0, 'alice'
1, 'bob'
2, 'catherine'
enumerate produces a list of tuples

zip combines multiple sequences into a single iterator.

This iterator generates a series of tuples containing elements from each iterable.
>>> s1 = {2, 3, 1}
>>> s2 = {'b', 'a', 'c'}
>>> list(zip(s1, s2))
[(1, 'a'), (2, 'c'), (3, 'b')]

sorted returns a sorted list, also has a reverse keyword if you need to reverse the result
reversed returns a reversed list
cycle from itertools is a useful standard library function that infinitely loops over a sequence of values
count from itertools provides a counter, which iterates by a step size every iteration
accumulate from itertools provides an accumulator, which aggregates successive values of a sequence. We can provide a function to define the accumulation function. The default is sum, but max is also useful accumulate(sequence, max)
chain from itertools will chain two sequences together. list(chain([1,2,3], "ABC")) yields [1,2,3,"A","B","C"]
dropwhile and takewhile from itertools are like filter. They will provide values until a trigger value is reached. Both require a predicate to check the values in the sequence.
groupby from itertools calculates the keys for each element present in iterable. It returns key and iterable of grouped items. This function takes two arguments: (1) the data to group and (2) the function to group it with.



Loops & control Flow

Standard conditionals control the logical branching of a program, these are the standard if, elif, else

if condition1:
    code
elif condition2:
    code2
else:
    code3

Loop with for, while

for i in iterator:
    code
while condition:
    code

Control the behaviour of loops with break, continue, pass

for number in range(10):
    if number == 5:
        pass    # pass here
By using the pass statement in this program, we notice that the program runs exactly as it would if there were no conditional statement in the program. The pass statement tells the program to disregard that condition and continue to run the program as usual.
for number in range(10):
    if number == 5:
        continue    # continue here
The continue statement gives you the option to skip over the part of a loop where an external condition is triggered, but to go on to complete the rest of the loop. That is, the current iteration of the loop will be disrupted, but the program will return to the top of the loop.
for number in range(10):
    if number == 5:
        break    # break here
In Python, the break statement provides you with the opportunity to exit out of a loop when an external condition is triggered. You’ll put the break statement within the block of code under your loop statement, usually after a conditional if statement.

Exception handling with try, except, raise

try, except and raise are used for exception handling. The program will begin by trying the code in the try block, but if an error is raised, it will run the code in the except block.
try:
  print(x)
except NameError:
  print("Variable x is not defined")
except:
  print("Something else went wrong") 
Multiple except statements can be used with specific errors like NameError, ValueError, TypeError,ZeroDivisionError.
The raise keyword will force a particular error to occur. Usually this is used to produce a specific error to inform the user

pattern matching is done with ‘match’

def check_value(value):
    match value:
        case 0:
            print("Value is zero")
        case 1:
            print("Value is one")
        case _:
            print("Value is something else")

check_value(0)  # Output: Value is zero
check_value(1)  # Output: Value is one
check_value(5)  # Output: Value is something else


Classes & objects

‘classes’ act as factories for generating objects (often called instances) and define unique types.
Classes may inherit from other classes (their parents), inheriting both data (fields) and behaviour (methods)
If B inherits from A, then an instance of B can be passed to something expecting A (subtyping)
An object should hide its data (encapsulation), which can only be operated on with methods.

Object-oriented design is then about identifying the classes (the ‘nouns’) and the methods (the ‘verbs’) and then establishing relationships between them, is-a and has-a.
Favour class composition over inheritance. Create more abstract classes by building them form less-abstract classes with has-a relationships.
Pythonic getters and setters with property decorator. properties should only be used when no calculation is performed i.e just simple getting of info. Use full method when some work is being done.
class House:

    def __init__(self, price):
        self._price = price

    @property
    def price(self):
        return self._price

    @price.setter
    def price(self, new_price):
        if new_price > 0 and isinstance(new_price, float):
            self._price = new_price
        else:
            print("Please enter a valid price")

    @price.deleter
    def price(self):
        del self._price
Special class methods allow one to implement particular operators for you custom class.

The most useful are __getitem__, __init__, __len__, __call__. These are called to the object using

object[i]
object = class(init_args)
len(object)
object(call_args)

custom iterator classes can be created by implementing __next__ and __iter__ methods. These return tell the functions next(x) and iter(x) what to do.

Advanced class methods

usually used to assign human-readable names to constant values in program. They have name and value properties. They are from the enum package of the standard library and created like

from enum import Enum
class Fruit(Enum):
    APPLE = 1
    BANANA = 2

Fruit.APPLE.name gives APPLE and Fruit.APPLE.value gives 1
String representations of classes can be defined by the __str__ and __repr__ methods. They tell the class what to output when str and repr functions are called on the object. the repr version is used for more detailed output for debugging, and str method is for short, human readable description.
We can add numeric-like functionality to classes by overriding the following methods: __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __div__, __floordiv__, __pow__, __and__ __or__. These allow the use of binary mathematical operators (like +, -,**) on your object. you can also use the in-place versions of these operations by overriding __iadd__ (for +=) etc.
We can do the same with comparison operators: __gt__, __lt__, __ge__, __le__, __eq__, __ne__ for operations like >, >=, == etc. These are useful as they allow the object to be sorted in collections.
__slots__ attribute in classes can be used to optimize classes. They allow you to explicitly state which instance attributes you expect your object instances to have, with the expected results:

faster attribute access.
space savings in memory.


class Base:
    __slots__ = 'foo', 'bar'
Abstract base classes
These are a way of defining templates for additional subclasses. We can enforce what methods are required when subclassing by using the Python abc module.
# Implementing Different Methods for Classes
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

#This is the template class
class Employee(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def arrive_at_work(self):
        pass

#These subclasses must implement the arrive_at_work method to avoid errors
class Manager(Employee):
    def arrive_at_work(self):
        print("Arriving at datagy.io headquarters!")

class Supervisor(Employee):
    def arrive_at_work(self):
        print("Reporting for duty at datagy.io!")

nik = Manager()
katie = Supervisor()

title: Python Notes
text:
Functional programming in python
Functional programming is a declarative programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions. It emphasises immutability, first-class functions, and the avoidance of side-effects.
In functional programming, functions are treated as first-class citizens, which means that they can be passed as arguments to other functions, returned as values from functions, and assigned to variables. This enables a style of programming in which functions are composed in a way that is similar to mathematical functions.
The key features of functional programming are

Pure functions

functions should never change the data in-place
functions should have no side effects
functions should have no access to external variables

Higher-order functions - can take functions as arguments or return them as results
Comprehensions
Lambda (anonymous) functions
Recursion
Immutable objects - a function should never change the data in-place

#an example of higher-order functions
def apply_twice(func, arg):
  return func(func(arg))

def add_five(x):
  return x + 5

print(apply_twice(add_five, 10))  # prints 20
#an example of function composition
from functools import reduce

def multiply_by_two(x):
  return x * 2

def add_three(x):
  return x + 3

def compose(f, g):
  return lambda x: f(g(x))

f = compose(multiply_by_two, add_three)
result = reduce(f, [1, 2, 3, 4], 0)
print(result)  # prints 20
#an example of immutability
def remove_duplicates(items):
  seen = set()
  for item in items:
    if item not in seen:
      seen.add(item)
      yield item

items = [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5]
result = list(remove_duplicates(items))
print(result)  # prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Key tools for functional python are, map, reduce , filter
Further functional programming tools are found in the functools and itertools modules.
The itertools module contains valuable functions such as count, cycle, repeat, product, permutations, combinations, accumulate, starmap.
The functools module is for higher-order functions. It includes lots of useful things for composing pure functions, such as reduce and partial.
The key sense of work in the functional paradigm is compositions of pure functions acting on iterables. A very valuable pattern is the map-reduce pattern. The map-reduce pattern is an abstract representation of many types of computations that manipulate lists or collections of objects. The map stage takes the input collection and maps it to an intermediate representation. The reduce step takes this intermediate representation and computes a single output from it.

title: Docker Notes
text:
Docker image: An executable package that contains everything needed to run an application
Docker container: A running docker image
Docker file: a file that describes the build of a docker image. Describes what goes on inside the environment of the container
Docker registry: a collection of docker repositories where we store docker images. We can push/pull images from the docker registry
Virtual machines load a guest OS on the machine. Each virtual machine has its own guest OS. Docker images by contrast use the docker daemon to interact with the host OS, and as such are much smaller and startup faster.

Docker file -> builds -> Docker image -> runs -> docker container
Key docker commands are

build : build an image from a dockerfile
push/pull : pushes, pulls images from a docker registry
image: commands for dealing with docker images
container: commands for dealing with docker containers (running instances for docker images)
login login to a docker registry


Docker files
Docker builds images by reading the instructions from a docker file in order. Docker files have several standard commands

FROM: build a docker image starting with another image, this is particularly useful for starting with an ubuntu distribution docker image as a basis and adding stuff on top.
EXPOSE indicates the ports on which the container listens for instructions
LABEL add information and useful metadata to the image.
WORKDIR specify the working directory for the following commands
COPY copies over files from the source to the filesystem of the container
RUN : run command-line commands. Usually we start with installing python libraries
CMD: tells the container what to do after launching. This defines a default. There can only be one CMD line in a dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT: An ENTRYPOINT allows you to configure a container that will run as an executable.

For example
FROM ubuntu:18.10
LABEL version="0.1"
WORKDIR /data
COPY . /data
RUN pip install pandas jupyter
EXPOSE 8888
CMD ["jupyter", "notebook", "--ip=0.0.0.0", "--port=8888", "--no-browser"]


Docker images
We build an image out of a dockerfile using
docker build -t imagename dockerfile
With images we can run commands like ls, rm. e.g. docker image ls -a
You can save docker images using docker save to a tar file. But the ideal senario is to share images using push/pull to the registry. to load a tarball image, use docker load < image.tar


Docker containers
We run a container using the command
docker container run -it imagename
The -it runs it interactively.
With containers we can also use commands like like ls, run, stop, kill, rm
We can also mount databases using docker volumes. These are bound to a docker container filesystem using the -v flag in container run.
We bind ports to a docker container using -p flag in container run

title: Graphs: A Primer
text:
These notes are asimple primer on the mathematical treament of graphs, particularly the spectral properties and how basic ML models incorporate graph data. The aim is to present a few notes on graph theory concepts, such as the adjacency matrix, Laplacian and incidence matrix. These will not be comprehensive, but rather a short reference. Lets start with a few definitions. A graph is a mathematical structure consisting of vertices (or nodes) and edges (connections between nodes). Graphs can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and can have various properties depending on their structure.


Simple graphs are defined as follows: * No loops (self-connections) * No multi-edges * Undirected (symmetric adjacency)
Let \(\mathcal{G} = \{ \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E} \}\), this is our graph, with:
\(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{G}) = \{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}\): vertex set of graph \(\mathcal{G}\), where \(n = |\mathcal{V}|\) \(\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{G}) = \{e_{ij}\}\): edge set with \(m = |\mathcal{E}|\)
Where an edge \(e_{ij}\) connects \(v_i\) to \(v_j\)



The degree of vertex \(v_i\) is the number of connections (neighbors):
\[
d(v_i) = \sum_j e_{ij}
\]

If all vertices have the same degree, the graph is regular
If all degrees are even, the graph is Eulerian




Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be a subgraph of \(\mathcal{G}\) if:
\[
\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{H}) \subseteq \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{G}), \quad \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{H}) \subseteq \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{G})
\]



A graph is k-partite if its vertex set admits a partition into \(k\) classes such that vertices in the same class are not adjacent.



Much of the mathematical treament of graphs starts with the adjacency matrix. This matrix is a way to represent the connections between vertices in a graph, where each row and column corresponds to a vertex, and the entries indicate whether there is an edge between the vertices.
For a graph of \(N\) vertices:
Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) where
\[
  A_{ij} =
  \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if there is an edge } e_{ij} \\
  0 & \text{if no edge}
  \end{cases}
\]
Also, \(A_{ii} = 0\)
Note: \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) for a weighted graph \(A \in \mathbb{B}^{N \times N}\) for an unweighted graph, where \(\mathbb{B} = \{0, 1\}\)
Thus the adjacency matrix describes the connections in the graph. For an undirected, weighted graph, the adjacency matrix \(A\) is:

A real symmetric matrix
Has \(N\) real eigenvalues
\(N\) eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis

Let the eigenspace be:
\[
S_i = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^N \ \middle| \ A x = \lambda_i x \right\}
\]



In addition to the adjacency matrix, we can also define functions on graphs. These are mappings from a vertex to a value. Consider a real-valued function on a graph:
\[
  f: \mathcal{V} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
\(f\) is a vector indexed by vertices: \(f \in \mathbb{R}^N\)

The eigenvectors can be considered as eigenfunctions
The adjacency matrix acts as a linear operator:

\[
  g = A f, \quad g_i = \sum_j A_{ij} f_j
\]



The adjacency operator can also be seen as a quadratic form:
\[
f^T A f = \sum_{e_{ij}} f_i f_j
\]



If we let the graph edges have an orientation, we can define an incidence matrix (operator):
\[
\nabla \in \mathbb{T}^{|E| \times |V|}, \quad \mathbb{T} = \{0, 1, -1\}
\]
Define \(\nabla\) as:
\[
\nabla_{ev} =
\begin{cases}
-1 & \text{if } v \text{ is source of } e \\
1 & \text{if } v \text{ is sink of } e \\
0 & \text{if no connection}
\end{cases}
\]
Directed graphs can be represented with an incidence matrix, where each edge has a direction (source to sink). The incidence matrix \(\nabla\) captures the relationship between edges and vertices in a concise way.



The incidence matrix is used in the definition of the coboundary ma. The mapping \(f \rightarrow \nabla f \in \mathbb{R}^{E}\) is the coboundary map of the graph and can be used to compute the gradient of a function defined on the graph.
\[
(\nabla f)(e_{ij}) = f(v_j) - f(v_i)
\]



Spectral graph theory studies properties of graphs via the eigensystem and their associated matrices. The key concept in the spectral graph theory is the Graph Laplacian. The Laplacian operator is defined as:
\[
L = \nabla^T \nabla
\]
Component-wise:
\[
(Lf)(v_i) = \sum_{e_{ij}} (f(v_i) - f(v_j))
\]
Also defined as:
\[
L = D - A
\] Where: * \(D\) is the degree matrix: \(D_{ii} = d(v_i)\) * Diagonal matrix with degrees at each vertex * \(A\) is the adjacency matrix For a weighted graph, each edge \(e_{ij}\) has a weight \(w_{ij}\), which modifies the Laplacian accordingly. Component form: \[
(Lf)(v_i) = \sum_{e_{ij}} w_{ij} (f(v_i) - f(v_j))
\] As a quadratic form: \[
f^T L f = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{e_{ij}} w_{ij} (f(v_i) - f(v_j))^2
\] * The Laplacian \(L\) is symmetric and positive-definite (or semi-definite) and so has non-negative, real-valued eigenvalues
The graph laplacian is a powerful tool in spectral graph theory, allowing us to analyze the structure and properties of graphs through their eigenvalues and eigenvectors. It is equivalent to the familiar laplacian operator in continuous spaces, but adapted to the discrete, arbitrarily-structured setting of graphs.



Just as with the Fourier transform in continuous spaces, we can define a Graph Fourier Transform for graphs. This allows us to analyze functions defined on the vertices of a graph in terms of the graph’s spectral properties. It is this transform that defines the spectral structure of the graph and allows us to decompose functions into their frequency components.

We can project a function (or signal) over the space of eigenvectors of a graph.
For eigenvectors \(\mu\) and eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of the Laplacian \(L\), the Graph Fourier Transform is defined as:

\[
\mathcal{F}(f)[\lambda_i] = \hat{f}(\lambda_i) = \langle f, \mu^i \rangle = \sum_{j=1}^{N} f_j \mu_j^i
\]
This gives:
\[
\hat{f} = \mu^T f \quad \text{(i.e., transform = basis projection)}
\]

title: Graphs: A Primer
text:
Models on Graphs
Graphs are a powerful data structure for representing relationships and structures in data. In machine learning, graphs can be used to model relationships between entities, such as social networks, molecular structures, or knowledge graphs. In the rest of these notes I will briefly introduce some of the basic models that operate on graph data:

Graph Convolutional Model (GCN)
Convolutional neural networks have long been the mainstay of deep learning for images and other grid-like or linear data. However, graphs present a challenge due to their irregular structure. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a class of neural networks designed to operate on graph-structured data. First introduced by Kipf and Welling (2016a), GCNs extend the concept of convolution to graphs by leveraging the graph structure to perform local aggregations of node features.

Approximates the graph Fourier transform using a neural network.
Can be an effective classifier for nodes in a graph.

A single GCN layer is:
\[
H^{(l+1)} = \sigma \left( \tilde{D}^{-1/2} \tilde{A} \tilde{D}^{-1/2} H^{(l)} W^{(l)} \right)
\]
Where:

\(\tilde{A} = A + I\): adjacency matrix with self-loops
\(\tilde{D}\): degree matrix of \(\tilde{A}\)
\(H^{(l)}\): input features at layer \(l\)
\(W^{(l)}\): learnable weight matrix
\(\sigma\): activation function (e.g. ReLU)
\(\tilde{A} = A + I\): adjacency matrix with self-connections added.
\(\tilde{D}^{-1/2} \tilde{A} \tilde{D}^{-1/2}\): symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix.
\(\tilde{D}\): degree matrix of \(\tilde{A}\), where:
\[
\tilde{D}_{ii} = \sum_j \tilde{A}_{ij}
\]
\(H^l\): activation (output) of the l-th GCN layer, with \(H^0 = X\) (input node features).
\(\sigma\): activation function, typically ReLU.

Thus a two-layer GCN would be:
\[
\text{GCN}_2(X, A) = \tilde{A} \, \sigma(\tilde{A} X W^0) W^1
\]


Graph Autoencoder (GAE)
We can go furhter and build more complex models out of our GCNs. A Graph Autoencoder (GAE) is a type of neural network that learns to encode graph data into a lower-dimensional space and then reconstructs the graph structure from this encoding. This is particularly useful for tasks like link prediction or node classification. This model was introduced in Kipf and Welling (2016b) and has found application in various domains, as well inspiring varaitional and other approaches to graph representation learning.

Goal: learn representations of nodes by reconstructing the adjacency matrix. This particular model is for binary adjacency matrices i.e. unweighted graphs.
Encoder: \[
Z = \text{GCN}_2(X, A)
\] \(Z\): latent (compressed) node features.
Decoder: \[
\tilde{A} = \sigma(ZZ^T)
\] Uses inner product decoder to reconstruct \(A\) (assumes \(\sigma\) is sigmoid).
\(Z\): gives latent space representations of the nodes.
To get graph-level representations (for small graphs), you can apply sum-pooling over node vectors:

\[
\sum Z
\]
So, for an unweighted, undirected graph \(G(V, E)\), with \(N = |V|\), the model derives a node feature matrix: \[
  X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times F}, \quad Z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}
\] from the adjacency matrix: \[
  A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} \text{ (weighted)}, \quad A \in \mathbb{B}^{N \times N} \text{ (unweighted)}
\]

Further Reading
A few key resources I found useful for graphs is the Graph Representation Learning book (Hamilton 2020). This book provides a comprehensive introduction to graph representation learning, covering both theoretical foundations and practical applications. There are also some nice review articles covering machine learning with graphs, such as Zhou et al. (2020). In terms of software packages, the networkx package in Python is a great library for working with graphs, providing tools for creating, manipulating, and analyzing graph structures. title: What is a literature review for?
text: A literature review forms the foundation of any research project, serving as both a learning tool and a roadmap for your academic journey. This is true for researchers and students of any level, but this is particularly true for graduate students starting off on their research career. Remember that it is primarily through reading the literature of a field that we become experts not only in the most recent results, but also the methods, trends and the academic community. Furthermore, by taking a step back and getting an expansive view of the key problems before jumping into your investigation, you prevent wasting your own time chasing false leads and unnecessary research directions. The literature review process helps researchers develop a deep understanding of their field before conducting original research. This critical step ensures your work builds upon existing knowledge while identifying genuine research gaps. Your review should demonstrate both breadth of knowledge and depth of understanding in your chosen area. Let’s explore each aspect in detail.

title: What is a literature review for?
text:
Consider your question
Your research question serves as the compass for your literature review. Possibly you have been provided with a central task, question or objective for your work, or perhaps you have been given free rein to come up with the subject of your thesis yourself. Either way it is paramount to firmly define what your work is about. Before diving into the literature, you need to frame your research question.
Firstly, consider whether you are solving a specific problem. Many fields have converged on particular problems; some will be famous with a history of defeating even the most ardent attempts at a solution. Others-and these are perhaps the more intriguing-lie unloved and somewhat orphaned, despite potentially showing the way to fertile pastures. The second type is investigating to discover something new. This is particularly true of ‘blue skies’ or exploratory research. Simply trying something out because you think it might be interesting or playing around in a less serious logic than the supposed coldness that people ascribe to the sciences. These last two paradigms represent what the mathematician Sir Michael Atiyah in Advice to a Young Mathematician called “problem solvers” or “theorists”. The former are motivated by the task of proving conjectures while the latter dedicate themselves to the development of theory. The third type I will identify is creating or developing something novel. This might be a technique, technology or tool. In truth most research is a mixture, and rarely does the initial question stay the same throughout a project.
In each case you should be able to write down a sentence describing your question, and indeed it helps to be in the form of a question, for the form of a question invites a kind of internal dialectic helpful when planning a project.

title: What is a literature review for?
text:
Searching for literature
The first stage is to hit the literature. Collect papers on the topic, especially review articles and the latest research. Another underused source is PhD theses and dissertations; these contain the results of previous graduate students’ attempts at chewing through the literature of a field. As such they are an invaluable source of references and background.
These days the field of helpful tools has expanded far beyond trawling through archives. Aside from Google scholar, there are many AI-powered services you can use to power your search. A few favourites are:

Elicit: Helps search and synthesize research findings and identify patterns across papers
Consensus: Search and aggregates scientific results on specific topics
PaperQA: Enables targeted questions about research papers
ConnectedPapers: Visualizes relationships between publications, including the most relevant and heavily cited works.
Mendeley: Reference manager and library for your collected articles
Zotero: Similar to Mendeley. Zotero, Mendeley and Google scholar allow one to export bibtex for reference management and writing. Scientific writing tools like latex require bibtex format references and it can be helpful to auto generate your project-specific references.

All of these can help you find and filter the most relevant literature for your problem. To filter the set of papers you have collected, first read the title and the abstract; if this seems promising and relevant, then read the conclusions and the figures. The sad reality is there has been an explosion in literature in the sciences, and keeping up with developments is a difficult task. One does not have the time to read every article in the field, even less to understand each fully. The key is filtering and selecting those upon which you can build an interesting and insightful research project of your own. The key object of the review exercise is to build an argument, not a library. For this purpose one must be selective and filter out only those articles that are most relevant. When you have selected your corpus, consider the following:

What has been left out?
Where does it lead?
What is/could be the next step?
What is the kernel of unevaluated science in this paper?

Also don’t forget the quality of the studies themselves, in particular consider the

Methodological strengths and limitations
Underlying assumptions
Potential applications to your research
Unexplored implications.

The rapid expansion of AI in recent years is a case in point. Some successful papers in the field have been the result of successfully expanding on appendices and ‘side’ experiments of previous papers. Consider that which one author might condemn to an appendix may be an incredibly insightful result with just some extra thought and effort.
You should at this stage have a set of key papers of interest to you. Briefly describe the background and context of these; after all, this context is also that of your work too. Define the objectives and key methods of these papers. What approaches did they use? Could you adopt or adapt them for your project too? Finally consider a small summary of the literature itself, with a paragraph for each of the main papers and how they contribute to your work. The review should have a narrative thread that leads to your research being a good idea. Again AI tools can help you with this, take full advantage of them, but remember this exercise is for your own benefit. It is for you to understand the state of the field.
Consider the people too, look at the various groups and individuals who are publishing relevant work. By reviewing literature we also come to know who are the ‘movers and shakers’ and the most influential labs. This is important because this is where you can find potential collaborators, reviewers, and possibly even your future colleagues.

title: What is a literature review for?
text:
Writing the review
Once you have compiled your corpus of literature it is time to put it all together. A basic introduction-body-conclusion structure will suffice. The introduction should establish your review’s focus, outline the scope of literature covered, and highlight the significance of your topic. Include your research question and briefly explain how you’ve broken down the review. In the body, for each key paper, provide:

Background and contextual information
Clear objectives and methodological approaches
Potential adaptations for your research
Critically evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of research method

The conclusion should synthesize the key findings, discuss their implications, and identify research gaps that justify your own study. Don’t worry about writing a comprehensive review of the whole field, and don’t spend too long describing the minutiae of competing methods. If all is well you will pick and choose parts of previous work to assemble your own approach.
A well-structured literature review for a scientific research project should follow a clear organizational framework that effectively synthesizes and analyses existing research. A well-crafted literature review does more than summarize existing research—it builds a compelling argument for your research direction while demonstrating your thorough understanding of the field’s current state. Lastly, and most importantly, it builds your own understanding and helps you devise your project’s direction.

title: Graphs of Neurological Terminology
text:
Understanding how neurological conditions are described in medical literature is critical for improving communication, advancing research, and enhancing patient care. Neurological descriptions often involve complex, nuanced language, which can obscure underlying relationships between conditions and treatments. By leveraging computational approaches to analyse these descriptions, we can uncover semantic patterns that enhance our understanding of neurological discourse. In this post I am going to describe some work I completed as part of a fellowship project this year. The aim is to build a network of terms from neurological descriptions using point-wise mutual information (PMI) and applies graphical modelling to identify key semantic structures. I isolate an ontological structure from reporting in an unsupervised manner, find key patterns of presentation, and find the key correlates of disorders with their description.
Unstructured text in radiological reports poses significant barriers to effective diagnosis and clinical standardisation. Neurological radiological reports, in particular, contain diverse terminology and data linked to complex conditions such as strokes and epilepsy. Despite their richness, these reports lack standardised frameworks for terminology usage, making it difficult to extract actionable insights or ensure consistency across clinical settings. Advances in natural language processing, particularly transformer-based models like BERT have shown promise in analysing medical texts. However while these approaches have been applied to general radiology or specific imaging modalities like chest X-rays, their application to neurological radiological reports remains limited.
A large part of the Guarantors of Brain project involved building tools for analysing and understanding the language used in neurological reports. A small part of which builds on prior work by integrating language model-derived embeddings with graph-based analytical techniques to uncover latent structures within neurological radiological reports. By identifying clusters of terms and analysing their relationships through co-occurrence graphs, we can reveal diagnostic patterns and terminology usage variations that can inform clinical practice and standardisation efforts. In this project, I find the distinct meta-language of neuroradiology. It aims to uncover diagnostic patterns and terminology usage in neurology by analysing co-occurrence graphs and clustering neurological terms.
In short, understanding latent structures in radiological reports can:
The approach begins with the extraction of terms and phrases from a corpus of neurological texts, followed by the computation of PMI to identify statistically significant co-occurrences of terms. These co-occurrences are represented as a weighted graph, where nodes are terms and weighted edges reflect their mutual information. A graph model is trained on this graph to identify higher-order structures and patterns. Semantic sub-networks can be extracted and analysed, focusing on the relationships between conditions, interventions, and descriptors. We extracted terms and phrases from a large corpus of neurological texts—including over 300,000 MRI head scans collected during 25 years of clinical practice at Queen Square—to capture the diverse language used in radiological reports. High PMI values might indicate meaningful relationships, such as common co-morbidities or symptom-disease relationships.
With the graph constructed, we can then move onto applying node clustering algorithms. I used soft Louvain clustering to identify communities within the network, allowing for the detection of non-exclusive thematic groups. Unlike traditional Louvain clustering, soft Louvain clustering ascribes a probability of membership to each node in the graph, therefore I can use this parameter to find non-exclusive communities of nodes in the graph. The value of non-exclusive community detection is that it allows each node to belong to more than one community. This is certainly the case for non-specific terminology such as “inflammation” that can co-occur alongside multiple different conditions or diagnoses. These communities might correspond to thematic areas within a corpus, such as specific branches of medicine or research clusters. Investigating these communities can reveal how different topics are interconnected and identify potential interdisciplinary research areas. A threshold was applied to aggregate nodes for clarity, while Eigenvector Centrality was used to pinpoint the most influential terms within each cluster. These high-centrality primary nodes served as the “head” terms in an ontology, with the associated clusters forming templates that describe pathological conditions, imaging presentations, and key anatomical locations.
In addition to community detection, other graph metrics such as the clustering coefficient can be applied to the terminology graph to uncover structure. High clustering coefficients suggest the presence of specialised subtopics or highly focused areas within the medical texts. These cliques could represent highly interconnected fields, such as specific diseases with multiple associated symptoms or treatments.

title: Graphs of Neurological Terminology
text:
Results
The analysis reveals distinct semantic clusters corresponding to different neurological conditions, such as oncological and degenerative diseases. Sub-networks highlight how oncological conditions are interrelated through shared descriptors, suggesting potential overlaps in diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Here I show four example sub-graphs extracted from the larger terminology graph.






Figure 1: Here we take the semantic sub-graph identified with the Meningioma term. This sub-graph represents the semantic network of terminology co-occurrent with meningiomas and their associated description and locations.



Figure 1 shows a large semantic sub-graph identified with the Meningioma term. The blue, red and pink nodes represent pathological, descriptive and location terms respectively. With this layout, we can identify the primary terminology concurrent with meningiomas (the direct connections to meningioma terms) and also the second-order terminology. Figure 2 shows the encephalitis group, which is a cluster of terms related to encephalitis, a condition characterised by inflammation of the brain.






Figure 2: This encephalitis group shows the key terminology that co-occurs alongside encephalitis. Note the key locations of the limbic system and cingulate gyri, both anatomical locations consistent with common presentations of this pathology.



Figure 3 shows the aneurysm sub-graph. This sub-graph is smaller and was extracted using a higher probability threshold in the Louvain community detection routine. As such, this group represents a much tighter terminology set associated with aneurysms. Figure 4 shows a small subset of the whole ontology created by identifying the high-centrality terms (which define sub-specialities) and their constituent terminology that defines their wider presentation. This method provides an entirely data-driven approach to creating ontologies directly from medical text, without the need for manual curation or a-priori input.






Figure 3: This aneurysm sub-graph shows the key terminology associated with the presentation of aneurysms in practice. One can see that coiling, a primary intervention used in the treatment of aneurysms, features prominently in the network.









Figure 4: The clustering and graphical structure allow us to create an automated ontology based on the structure and centrality terms. Here a subset of the clusters, identified by their most important term, shows the sub-nodes that exemplify their presentation.









Figure 5: The demyelination group shows a short graph distance to terms involved in small vessel disease and ischaemia, this is not unsuprising given their similar appearances on imaging.









Figure 6: The stroke group shows the key terminology in the centre, in this case ‘infarction’ and ‘haemorrhage’, with the associated descriptive and anatomical terms.



By identifying key semantic structures in neurological descriptions, this approach provides insights into medical language that can improve patient care and support research. This method is also flexible enough to be applied to other domains of medical and scientific text, bridging the gap between unstructured data and actionable knowledge. With this approach, I can (1) identify clusters of related terms and provide insights into diagnostic patterns that can aid clinicians in recognising complex conditions more effectively. (2) The observed inconsistencies underscore the need for standardised medical language across clinical settings. Standardization could improve communication among healthcare professionals and reduce diagnostic variability. (3) Insights from co-occurrence graphs can inform better knowledge representation within EHR systems by highlighting key terms and their relationships. (4) Variations in terminology usage across demographics suggest potential biases that should be addressed to ensure equitable care. (5) Expanding this approach to other medical domains or integrating multimodal data (e.g., imaging features) could further enhance its applicability. Additionally, exploring advanced graph neural networks could provide deeper insights into term interconnections.
The full report and further details can be found in our preprint, (Watkins 2025).
